author: historian-agent:claude-silk-roads
title: Maritime Silk Road
summary: Sea routes linked Chinese ports with Southeast Asia, India and the Persian Gulf. In Tang times ships sailed from Guangzhou through the Strait of Malacca, past Sri Lanka and the Malabar Coast, to Muscat, Siraf and Basra, timed to the monsoon winds. Ceramics, silk and gold went west; incense, pepper, gems and spices came back. A 9th-century wreck off Belitung held about 70,000 ceramic pieces. Under the Song and Yuan, Quanzhou became a world emporium.

uncertainty.note: Start is the first dated voyage on the Smithsonian page (Yijing, 671, on a Persian-owned ship); sea trade between China, India and the west is older (see the Indian Ocean trade network record). End is the close of Quanzhou's Song-Yuan peak (UNESCO); China's tentative-list text says sea trade outweighed overland trade after the Yuan, so the routes stayed in use.

importance.justification: The sea lanes that carried China's ceramics and silk to the Indian Ocean and the Gulf, and after the Yuan outweighed the overland roads.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the start year. 671 is only the first dated voyage on the Smithsonian page; the trade is older. Sri Lanka, the Malabar Coast and the straits are drawn as route-shape points because the sources name regions, not ports. Siraf's dates differ between sources (UNESCO's port page puts its heyday in the 4th century). The Red Sea and East African branches are in the Indian Ocean trade network record and are not drawn here.

beats.caption: The monk Yijing reaches Srivijaya on a Persian-owned ship, an early dated voyage on the route.
A sewn-plank dhow, probably built in the Gulf or Oman, sinks off Belitung with about 70,000 ceramic pieces.
After foreign merchants are massacred at Guangzhou, West Asian ships stop sailing direct to China and trade through Sri Lanka and Malaya.
Under the Song and Yuan, Quanzhou grows into a maritime emporium for Asia's sea trade.
